title: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism

cards.h: Why workers fought each other in 1914
cards.b: Why did the proletariat of Europe march to war in 1914 instead of rising against it? Lenin's Imperialism (1916) is the answer: capitalism had changed into a new stage of monopolies and colonies, and bought off part of its workers. It also provided the left's way of reading global poverty.

Lenin wrote in Zurich in 1916, relying on J.A. Hobson's Imperialism (1902) and Rudolf Hilferding's Finance Capital (1910), and on Bukharin. Europe had divided Africa (Berlin Conference 1884-85) and most of Asia. Great powers armed. The pamphlet was subtitled "a popular outline".

Lenin lists five marks of imperialism: - Concentration of production into monopolies. - Merger of bank and industrial capital into finance capital, ruled by a financial oligarchy. - Export of capital, not just goods. - International monopolist combines dividing the world. - The territorial division of the world among the great powers.

Super-profits from colonies let capitalists pay a layer of workers better, making them conservative: the "labour aristocracy". That explains reformism and the Second International's betrayal of 1914. Engels had noted something similar for Britain. Lenin urged revolutionaries to split from such leaders.

War among imperialist powers, Lenin argued, produces crises that allow revolution where the system is weakest: Russia. He also backed national self-determination for colonies (1914 essay, The Right of Nations to Self-Determination), making anti-colonial movements allies of socialism. The Comintern (1919) and the Baku Congress of the Peoples of the East (1920) followed.

Leninist anti-imperialism drew in Ho Chi Minh, Mao, and many Asian and African leaders, and created Soviet aid in the Cold War. Yet the USSR itself held an empire: the Baltics were annexed in 1940, Eastern Europe came under Soviet control, and the invasions of Hungary (1956), Czechoslovakia (1968), and Afghanistan (1979) showed the limits of anti-imperial principle. Critics call that "Soviet social-imperialism" (Maoist phrase).

Economists: most capital exports before 1914 went to other rich or settler countries, not to poor colonies; Britain's trade with the colonies was a modest share. Kautsky (1914) said "ultra-imperialism", a peaceful cartel of powers, was possible. Schumpeter (1919) held that imperialism was a relic of pre-capitalist militarism, not capitalism. Historians (Robinson and Gallagher, "Imperialism of Free Trade", 1953) stress strategy and local crises. Post-colonial scholars say Lenin underestimates colonised people's agency and racism. Yet Marxist defenders say the theory predicted the scramble and unequal exchange.

Lenin's account fits the drain theory of Naoroji and R.C. Dutt. M.N. Roy's thesis in 1920 held that colonial profits sustained European labour. The CPI called Indian independence in 1947 "false" for a time (the Ranadive line of 1948-50), reading the national bourgeoisie as a junior partner of imperialism. Later debates in the "Mode of Production in Indian Agriculture" (1970s) and Prabhat Patnaik's work on neo-colonial finance continue the framework.

Key takeaways

  1. Imperialism (1916) links monopoly capitalism and colonial expansion.
  2. Five features: monopolies, finance capital, capital export, cartels, territorial division.
  3. The labour aristocracy explains reformism.
  4. The theory justified anti-colonial alliances and the weakest-link strategy.
  5. Critics: capital flows went mostly to rich countries; imperialism is not a necessary stage.

Debate questions

  1. Is imperialism a feature of capitalism or of states?
  2. Does the theory explain modern global inequality?
